toolInstruction: Use these entries as structured coaching knowledge. Keep final advice grounded in the player's real telemetry, preferences, and recent run context. Prefer concrete next-session actions over generic motivation, and avoid claiming a flaw is present unless the local analytics already suggest it. Treat the linked flaw, mechanics, scenarios, and evidence as support material for the final answer.

entries.title: Move the speed-accuracy balance back toward clean arrivals
entries.summary: When clicking runs are fast but messy, the player often needs cleaner deceleration and first-shot quality before trying to raise tempo again.
why: Clicking scores improve fastest when the arrive-and-fire pattern is repeatable.
A slightly slower first move with a cleaner first shot usually beats a fast miss plus correction.
actions: Run a block where every rep is judged by first-shot quality, not raw pace.
Brake a little earlier and keep the cursor path simple instead of snapping through the target.
When tempo returns, add it in small steps without giving back clean arrival quality.

drills.label: Precision clicking
drills.reason: Precision-first scenarios reinforce landing quality and reduce extra cleanup shots.

avoid: Forcing more tempo before arrival quality is stable
Do not increase difficulty purely because the run felt fast.
Avoid mixing too many wildly different click tasks in the same corrective block.

flaw.title: High correction load
flaw.summary: The player reaches the target area but spends too much extra motion cleaning up the hit.
telltales: Extra cleanup shots after otherwise decent acquires

contraindications: Do not assume every miss is a speed problem
avoid: Forcing more tempo before arrival quality is stable

mechanics.title: Deceleration and clean arrival
mechanics.summary: Braking early enough that the cursor finishes on target instead of through target.
cues: Brake sooner
Let the cursor arrive on target cleanly
failureModes: Overshooting and fixing it with extra cleanup movement

scenarios.name: Precision clicking block
scenarios.summary: A block that reinforces clean landing quality and lower correction pressure.
cautions: Return tempo gradually so arrival quality does not collapse immediately

evidence.claim: Clicking speed should be rebuilt on top of clean arrival quality, not in place of it.

entries.title: Build slow correction quality before adding snap
entries.summary: In control tracking, readable nonlinear direction changes are most useful when you let them teach accurate, gradual corrections first and only add speed once those corrections are reliable.
why: Gradual direction changes give you time to make the correction correctly instead of forcing a guess.
The category is useful because it punishes inaccurate corrections early, which exposes weak fundamentals fast.
actions: Start each direction-change correction slower than you think you need, then add speed only after the path stays clean.
If you are missing the majority of corrections back to the target, lower your pace until those corrections land reliably.
Use readable control tracking tasks as foundation work before expecting extreme reactive tasks to improve cleanly.

drills.label: Control tracking wrist
drills.reason: These tasks isolate readable corrections and make rushed, inaccurate direction changes obvious.

avoid: Using snappier corrections before consistency is built
Do not try to look snappy before the correction path is accurate.
Avoid treating punish-heavy control scenarios like pure speed tests.

flaw.title: Direction-change corrections are rushed
flaw.summary: The player tries to snap back to target too aggressively before the correction path is stable, especially on readable but nonlinear strafes.
telltales: Most corrections after direction changes miss or wobble
Corrections get faster before they get accurate
contraindications: Do not chase speed if the majority of corrections still fail
avoid: Using snappier corrections before consistency is built

mechanics.title: Slow, consistent corrections
mechanics.summary: When direction changes are readable, the player should first build accurate corrections at a slower pace and only add snap once those corrections land reliably.
cues: Start slower on direction changes
Only speed up after the correction path is reliable
Let the target punish bad corrections instead of hiding them with more force
failureModes: Trying to brute-force speed before the correction path is accurate
Missing the majority of adjustments back to target

evidence.claim: Control tracking should start with slow, strong corrections before speed is layered on.
evidence.excerpt: You have to start out slow and develop those strong foundations for fundamental corrections before speeding up.

entries.title: Blend muscle groups instead of isolating them
entries.summary: Control tracking is most effective when smaller groups start the movement and larger groups continue it, rather than pretending arm, wrist, or fingertips operate alone.
why: No useful aiming task is truly one isolated muscle group, so training quality depends on smooth handoff and overlap.
The blending category is valuable because it exposes delays or segmentation between movement layers.
actions: Think in terms of primary driver plus support, not exclusive muscle-group use.
On a small correction that grows wider, let the smaller group start the move and the larger group follow through without a pause.
Use fingertip or blending tasks to sharpen the handoff between movement scales, not to ban the other groups.

avoid: Trying to isolate one muscle group completely
Do not interpret a subcategory name as permission to use only one group.
Avoid obvious pauses when changing from a micro-correction into a larger follow-through.

entries.title: Place the crosshair where the target will be
entries.summary: The linear dynamic subcategory improves fastest when you reduce the physical gap between your crosshair and the target by leading its future path instead of reacting to its current position.
why: Large gains in dynamic clicking come from shrinking how far the mouse needs to move before the click.
Leading and then gradually reducing how much you lead builds both anticipation and timing quality.
actions: Aim at the target's future position instead of its current position on linear dynamic tasks.
Actively practice reducing the distance you lead by as your timing improves.
If your cursor is always trailing the bot, treat that as a placement problem before a flick-speed problem.

drills.label: Dynamic clicking linear
drills.reason: These tasks isolate the placement skill by rewarding future-position aiming over reactive chasing.

avoid: Always reacting to the target's current position
Do not always react to the target's present location.
Avoid over-leading so much that your timing becomes late in the opposite direction.

flaw.title: Target leading is weak
flaw.summary: The player keeps aiming at where the target is instead of where it will be, forcing larger corrective movement in dynamic clicking.
telltales: The cursor constantly trails the target path
Each click needs a larger correction than the target motion really demands
contraindications: Do not over-lead so much that timing becomes the next problem
avoid: Always reacting to the target's current position

mechanics.title: Lead placement
mechanics.summary: In dynamic clicking, the crosshair should be placed where the target will be rather than where it currently is, shrinking the physical gap the mouse must close.
cues: Place the crosshair ahead of the target path
Reduce the physical gap between crosshair and target
As the read improves, lead less while still staying ahead of the motion
failureModes: Flicking to the target's current position every time
Leading too far because the shot timing is not yet calibrated

entries.title: Move only as much as the target path actually demands
entries.summary: Precision click timing becomes much cleaner when you treat small, fast target motions as invitations to reduce displacement rather than to force bigger movement.
why: Readable precision tasks reward cursor paths that stay near center mass and avoid unnecessary travel.
Extra movement makes small targets and short strafes much harder than they need to be.
actions: On short, quick target motions, ask whether you can move less and still stay on a hittable line.
Bias toward center mass and simple cursor paths rather than chasing perfect-looking but oversized motions.
If precision tasks feel hectic, check whether your cursor is traveling farther than the target path requires.

drills.label: Dynamic clicking precision
drills.reason: These tasks reward minimal displacement and expose oversized movement on small readable paths.

avoid: Adding travel distance when a smaller correction would work
Do not add travel distance when the bot only moved a little.
Avoid turning compact motion into a full-sized flick out of habit.

flaw.title: Mouse displacement is larger than necessary
flaw.summary: The player moves more than the target path actually calls for, which hurts precision clicking and increases cleanup work.
telltales: Short target motions produce oversized cursor motions
Precision tasks feel harder because the cursor rarely stays near center mass
contraindications: Do not confuse bigger movement with better commitment
avoid: Adding travel distance when a smaller correction would work

mechanics.title: Minimal displacement
mechanics.summary: Precision clicking improves when the player moves the mouse only as much as the target path actually requires, keeping the cursor closer to center mass.

Stay as close to center mass as possible
Reduce unnecessary travel on small, quick movements

entries.title: Treat reading-heavy click timing as a prediction task, not just a click task
entries.summary: Reading-focused dynamic clicking is partly about hitting the target and partly about correctly understanding the arc or larger pattern before you commit.
why: The category builds both micro reading of individual paths and macro reading of the whole map pattern.
If the read is wrong, extra flick speed does not solve the real issue.
actions: Before each click, ask whether you truly understand the target's arc or are just reacting late to what you already missed.
On multi-target arc tasks, practice tracking the overall map pattern in your peripheral vision instead of tunneling on one target at a time.
Use reading-heavy click timing to train prediction quality before trying to brute-force faster clicks.

drills.label: Dynamic clicking reading
drills.reason: These tasks expose whether the miss came from weak prediction or from pure execution.

avoid: Treating a reading-heavy pattern like a simple static timing task
Do not reduce reading tasks to pure flick speed.
Avoid tunnel vision when the challenge is to read several arcs at once.

contraindications: Do not reduce this to only flick speed or click speed
avoid: Treating a reading-heavy pattern like a simple static timing task

mechanics.title: Arc reading

entries.title: Start braking earlier after target recognition
entries.summary: When recognition clearly happens before slowdown, the player is seeing the new path in time but beginning deceleration too late.
why: This is often a movement-chain timing issue, not a perception issue.
Earlier braking reduces both overshoot and follow-up correction work.
actions: Run one constraint block where the main goal is to start braking as soon as the new target path is recognized.
Treat recognition and slowdown as one linked skill instead of separate phases.
If braking starts late only at high tempo, lower tempo slightly until the timing relationship stabilizes.

drills.label: Recognition to decel drill
drills.reason: These reps train the exact gap between seeing the answer and beginning the controlled movement.

avoid: Pushing tempo higher before the recognition-braking link is stable
Do not interpret every late brake as slow reactions if the target was recognized in time.

avoid: Pushing tempo higher before the recognition-braking link is stable

entries.title: Balance family exposure so gains transfer better
entries.summary: If practice is dominated by one family, the player may build narrow strength that does not hold up well in other aim demands.
why: Transfer usually improves when the player keeps one strong family while feeding a smaller contrast family alongside it.
The goal is not equal time everywhere; it is enough contrast to stop adaptation from becoming too narrow.
actions: Keep the main family as the anchor, then add one supporting family that challenges the opposite weakness.
Review the weakest family for movement qualities that are missing from the main block.
Use contrast work consistently for a week before judging whether it is helping.

avoid: Treating equal time in every family as the goal

entries.title: Protect chaining before chasing flashier flick speed
entries.summary: Flick technique should develop speed in a productive way, where the initial flick lands cleanly and the full kill sequence stays efficient, rather than rewarding brute-force movement.
why: Fast flicks do not matter if they create unstable landings, slower target exits, or extra micro-correction.
Chaining is a better measure of flick quality than isolated flick speed because it captures what happens across multiple kills.
actions: Judge your kill sequences by clean first-shot hits and efficient transitions, not only by how fast the first movement felt.
If you are struggling on speed subcategories, ask which part of the kill chain is failing before trying to flick even faster.
In stability-biased tasks, actively slow down slightly if that helps you stop missing the initial flick.

drills.label: Flick technique stability
drills.reason: These tasks shift emphasis toward clean chaining and punish sloppy first flicks.

avoid: Trading away first-shot accuracy for a bit more raw speed
Do not use brute-force speed as the default answer.
Avoid sacrificing initial flick accuracy just to feel faster.

flaw.title: Chaining is weaker than raw flick speed
flaw.summary: The player may have fast single flicks, but the full kill sequence breaks because of misses, extra micro-adjustments, or poor exits.

contraindications: Do not judge flick quality only by one isolated fast movement
avoid: Trading away first-shot accuracy for a bit more raw speed

Leave each target in a way that sets up the next kill cleanly

entries.title: Train what happens after the flick, not only the flick itself
entries.summary: Post-flick tasks are valuable because they force large flick speed, immediate stability, and tension control to coexist inside the same rep.
why: What happens immediately after the large flick is often the real scoring bottleneck.
The best post-flick players still flick quickly, but they release tension soon enough to stabilize or track immediately.
actions: After each large flick, pay attention to whether you can settle or track immediately without an extra wobble.
Use post-flick tasks to practice releasing tension before the landing rather than after the miss happens.
Treat the follow-up stability as part of the flick skill, not a separate afterthought.

Trying to force more tempo while correction load is high often makes the movement chain noisier, not faster.
actions: Run a short block where the goal is one clean arrive-and-fire pattern, even if tempo dips slightly.
Brake a little earlier and let the cursor finish on target instead of through target.
Use slightly easier target sizes first if needed, but keep the movement pattern strict.

entries.title: Clean up delayed commit timing

why: Hesitation wastes already-correct aim by delaying the click or release decision.
Commit timing issues often feel like confidence problems, not mechanical inability.
actions: Run short blocks where you accept slightly lower accuracy in exchange for cleaner, earlier decisions.
Use a simple acquire -> commit -> fire rhythm and keep the cadence consistent for a full block.

entries.title: Shorten the warm-up tax before serious scoring runs
entries.summary: If early runs consistently underperform the settled part of the session, the player is paying a warm-up tax that burns good reps before quality is high enough.
why: Long warm-up ramps make peak performance harder to reach inside short practice blocks.
A predictable pre-routine is usually more valuable than adding more random warm-up volume.
actions: Build a fixed 5-10 minute opener with one easy tracking drill, one click-timing drill, and one scenario near your target task.
Do not start score attempts until movement quality and commit timing both feel stable for two consecutive runs.
If the first serious run is still weak, trim variety before adding duration.

entries.title: Exploit current momentum with nearby transfer work
entries.summary: When momentum is positive, the best move is often to expand slightly from the current strength rather than making a huge jump away from it.
why: Momentum is easiest to convert when the next task is close enough to reuse current movement quality.
Huge jumps in task demand can waste an otherwise productive session.
actions: Follow a strong block with one nearby transfer scenario that asks for slightly more speed, smaller targets, or faster recognition.
Keep the transfer task close enough that the same movement standard still makes sense.
If the transfer block collapses immediately, the jump was probably too large.

flaw.title: Momentum is not being converted into transfer
flaw.summary: Good current form is wasted because the next block is too unrelated or too large a jump away from the current strength.
telltales: Strong form disappears after one unrelated block
Transfer task jumps are too large to hold current quality
contraindications: Do not mistake randomness for useful challenge
avoid: Swapping into an unrelated hard task just because form feels good

mechanics.title: Near-transfer progression
mechanics.summary: Expand from current form with nearby task demands rather than huge unrelated difficulty jumps.
cues: Use one nearby transfer block after strong form
Keep the movement standard mostly the same
failureModes: Wasting good momentum on an unrelated or overly large jump

scenarios.name: Near-transfer block
scenarios.summary: A follow-up block that asks for a slightly harder version of the current successful movement pattern.
cautions: Keep the jump close enough that the current movement standard still applies

evidence.claim: Strong current form is best converted by nearby transfer work rather than unrelated challenge jumps.
evidence.excerpt: Hand-authored seed knowledge from the initial AimMod coaching model.

entries.title: In reactive tracking, land the correction before you push the pace
entries.summary: Manageable reactive tasks improve in-game aim best when you use them to make accurate repeated corrections, not to brute-force extreme reactivity.
why: More manageable reactive tasks often transfer to in-game aim better than extreme reactive gauntlets because you can actually train consistent adjustment quality inside them.
If your corrections miss most of the time, more speed only rehearses bad timing and bad landings.
actions: Use reactive categories to train repeated accurate corrections, not only raw reaction speed.
If you are missing the majority of corrections back to target, slow down until those corrections land.
Once consistency improves, add speed gradually instead of forcing it all at once.

drills.label: Reactive tracking control
drills.reason: These tasks preserve enough manageability to actually train repeatable adjustment quality.

avoid: Using snappier corrections before consistency is built
Do not treat extreme reactive difficulty as automatically better for improvement.
Avoid trying to out-speed a scenario you cannot yet control.

flaw.title: Direction-change corrections are rushed
flaw.summary: The player tries to snap back to target too aggressively before the correction path is stable, especially on readable but nonlinear strafes.
telltales: Most corrections after direction changes miss or wobble
Corrections get faster before they get accurate
contraindications: Do not chase speed if the majority of corrections still fail
avoid: Using snappier corrections before consistency is built

mechanics.title: Slow, consistent corrections
mechanics.summary: When direction changes are readable, the player should first build accurate corrections at a slower pace and only add snap once those corrections land reliably.
cues: Start slower on direction changes
Only speed up after the correction path is reliable
Let the target punish bad corrections instead of hiding them with more force
failureModes: Trying to brute-force speed before the correction path is accurate
Missing the majority of adjustments back to target

scenarios.name: Reactive tracking control
scenarios.summary: Manageable reactive tracking tasks where consistency and accuracy of adjustments matter more than extreme difficulty.
cautions: Slow down if most corrections back to target are still missing

scenarios.name: Reactive tracking speed
scenarios.summary: Reactive tasks where higher adjustment speed is required, but only in a way that still preserves clean control and deceleration.
cautions: Do not push speed by sacrificing the majority of your correction accuracy

scenarios.name: Reactive tracking reading
scenarios.summary: Reactive tasks that isolate reading of acceleration or strafe changes while still demanding snappy but accurate corrections.
cautions: The goal is not only to react faster but to read better before the correction

evidence.claim: The most important skill in reactive tracking is still the consistency of your adjustments.
evidence.excerpt: I still believe the consistency of your adjustments to be the most important skill here.

entries.title: Use reactive speed work to clean up tension, not to hide it
entries.summary: Reactive speed tasks expose whether your wrist and hand can decelerate and stabilize cleanly at higher speeds without locking up.
why: Higher adjustment speed only helps if tension is released early enough for controlled follow-through and micro-correction.
Reactive tasks can reveal lockout fast because the player must switch from a fast adjustment speed to a slower controlled tracking speed seamlessly.
actions: Pay attention to whether your wrist is responsible for the follow-through and whether tension makes it stick.
Choose a sensitivity where you can stay mobile rather than locked, then gradually push speed from there.
If your landing gets worse as speed rises, test whether the real issue is unbroken tension instead of under-commitment.

drills.label: Reactive tracking speed
drills.reason: The faster reactive tasks reveal whether your deceleration and follow-through stay mobile under pressure.

avoid: Holding speed tension all the way through the landing
Do not use more speed to hide a lockout problem.
Avoid treating a tense landing as a sign that you merely need more aggression.

flaw.title: Tension causes lockout
flaw.summary: The player holds too much tension during higher-speed adjustments or flicks, limiting smooth deceleration, micro-adjustment, and follow-through.
telltales: The wrist feels stuck during faster reactive or post-flick tasks
Landings become unstable because tension stays high too long
contraindications: Do not push sensitivity or speed higher if tension is already the bottleneck
avoid: Holding speed tension all the way through the landing

mechanics.title: Tension management
mechanics.summary: Snappier movement only helps if the player can release tension early enough to avoid lockout and recover into controlled follow-throughs or micro-adjustments.
cues: Release tension early in the flick
Monitor wrist lockout when higher-speed adjustments are needed
Let speed increases happen in sync with better control
failureModes: Holding tension too long through the follow-through
Locking the wrist when trying to go faster

scenarios.name: Reactive tracking speed
scenarios.summary: Reactive tasks where higher adjustment speed is required, but only in a way that still preserves clean control and deceleration.
cautions: Do not push speed by sacrificing the majority of your correction accuracy

evidence.claim: Reactive speed work sharpened tension awareness because of the need for snappier movement and wrist-driven follow-through.
evidence.excerpt: I had to be very conscious of my tension to avoid lockout.

entries.title: Rebuild retention with lighter re-entry sessions
entries.summary: If form drops hard after time away, the player may need a better re-entry structure instead of expecting immediate return to peak pace.
why: Retention improves when the first session back rebuilds movement quality before score pressure.
Expecting peak pace immediately after a gap often turns the first session into noisy recalibration.
actions: Make the first session back a re-entry session with slightly easier pacing and strict movement standards.
Use familiar scenarios first, then add one transfer scenario after quality stabilizes.
Judge the first session after a gap by regained feel, not peak score.

drills.label: Re-entry block
drills.query: return to aim training after break
drills.reason: A softer return preserves quality and improves next-day retention.

avoid: Using hardest tasks first after a gap
Do not compare the first post-gap session directly to your hottest recent peak.

flaw.title: Retention after a break is weak
flaw.summary: Form drops hard after time away because the player re-enters with too much score pressure and too little recalibration.
telltales: First session back feels noisy and over-pressured
Peak pace is expected before feel is rebuilt
contraindications: Do not compare the first session back to the best recent hot streak
avoid: Using hardest tasks first after a gap

mechanics.title: Re-entry structure after a break
mechanics.summary: The first session after time away should rebuild feel and movement quality before score pressure ramps up.
cues: Start with familiar tasks
Judge regained feel before judging peak score
failureModes: Expecting immediate peak pace after a gap

scenarios.name: Re-entry block
aliases: return to aim training after break
scenarios.summary: A first-session-back structure that rebuilds feel before score pressure ramps up.
cautions: Do not start with the hardest scenarios after a break

evidence.claim: The first session after a gap should rebuild feel before it chases peak scores.
evidence.excerpt: Hand-authored seed knowledge from the initial AimMod coaching model.

entries.title: Give the recovery phase a cleaner target
entries.summary: If recovery and stabilization are weak, the player may be handling the initial move well enough but failing to settle quickly after correction or direction change.
why: Recovery quality determines whether one mistake becomes a small delay or a full rhythm break.
Many players improve faster by cleaning recovery than by forcing a better first move.
actions: Use short blocks that deliberately emphasize smooth settle-after-correction behavior.
Keep the mouse pressure low during the settle phase to avoid a second correction spike.
Review whether recovery failures happen more after misses, target switches, or fast reversals.

drills.label: Recovery block
drills.reason: Stabilization-focused reps make post-correction rhythm easier to clean up.

avoid: Holding too much tension during settle phases
Do not only analyze the first error; the recovery quality afterward matters just as much.

flaw.title: Stabilization and recovery are noisy
flaw.summary: The initial error may be manageable, but the settle-after-correction phase is too slow or unstable.
telltales: One correction leads to a second wobble
Mistakes break rhythm longer than they should
contraindications: Do not only analyze the first miss and ignore the recovery phase
avoid: Holding too much tension during settle phases

mechanics.title: Post-correction stabilization
mechanics.summary: After a correction or reversal, the player should settle quickly without introducing a second wobble.
cues: Keep pressure low during the settle phase
Judge recovery quality separately from the initial miss
failureModes: One mistake becoming a full rhythm break because recovery stays noisy

scenarios.name: Recovery block
scenarios.summary: A block that focuses on clean settle-after-correction behavior.
cautions: Judge the settle quality, not only the initial miss rate

evidence.claim: Recovery quality is a separate and coachable part of the movement chain.
evidence.excerpt: Hand-authored seed knowledge from the initial AimMod coaching model.

entries.title: Reduce the switch penalty between scenario families
entries.summary: If performance drops after changing task types, the player may be carrying the previous rhythm and timing model into the next scenario.
why: Good mechanics do not transfer automatically if the player fails to reset pacing and commit expectations.
Interleaving works best when each block starts with a deliberate reset, not a rushed carryover.
actions: Before the first run in a new family, state the new target behavior in one sentence: smooth follow, clean first-shot, or rapid confirm-and-switch.
Use very short transition blocks when changing scenario families instead of instantly score chasing.
Track whether the penalty is worse in one direction, such as tracking into clicking or vice versa.

drills.label: Interleaving block
drills.reason: Structured switching builds adaptation without letting the old tempo leak into the new task.

avoid: Switching task families with no reset at all
Do not judge transfer quality from the very first rushed rep after a hard scenario switch.

flaw.title: Switch penalty between families
flaw.summary: Performance drops when moving between scenario families because the previous rhythm carries over into the next task.
telltales: First reps after a family change feel mechanically wrong
One direction of transition is much worse than the other
contraindications: Do not judge transfer from a rushed first rep after a hard switch
avoid: Switching task families with no reset at all

mechanics.title: Context reset between task families
mechanics.summary: A short reset helps the player switch timing models instead of carrying one scenario's rhythm into the next.
cues: State the target behavior before the first rep
Use a short reset block after a hard family switch
failureModes: Dragging tracking rhythm into clicking or vice versa

scenarios.name: Interleaving block
scenarios.summary: A short switching structure that trains context reset and cleaner family transitions.
cautions: Do not make the switches so fast that no real adaptation happens

evidence.claim: Scenario switching improves more from deliberate reset behavior than from blind repetition.
evidence.excerpt: Hand-authored seed knowledge from the initial AimMod coaching model.

entries.title: Prioritize smooth control over aggressive chase behavior
entries.summary: Tracking players with overshoot bursts or unstable contact usually need smoother matching and earlier deceleration rather than more reactive intensity.
why: In tracking, every overshoot burst creates recovery gaps where score leaks continuously.
Control improvements usually raise both contact quality and later pace ceiling.
actions: Use a lighter grip and focus on matching target speed exactly instead of chasing late.
Start with larger or slower tracking variants if needed, but hold a strict smoothness standard.
If contact breaks repeatedly near direction changes, train braking and re-acceleration as one movement.

drills.label: Smooth tracking block
drills.query: smooth tracking large target slow tracking
drills.reason: These reps reinforce stable contact and lower overshoot pressure.

avoid: Overgripping to force smoothness
Do not benchmark tracking quality only by peak speed if contact quality is unstable.
Avoid overgripping to force control; it usually creates more jitter.

flaw.title: Tracking control foundation is unstable
flaw.summary: Continuous target contact breaks down because the player chases late or over-corrects during direction changes.
telltales: Overshoot bursts during target direction changes
Contact quality collapses when pace rises
contraindications: Do not use peak speed as the only quality measure
avoid: Overgripping to force smoothness

mechanics.title: Speed matching
mechanics.summary: Tracking quality improves when the player matches target speed smoothly instead of chasing late.
cues: Escort the target
Keep grip pressure low while maintaining contact
failureModes: Aggressive chase behavior that creates overshoot bursts

mechanics.title: Deceleration and clean arrival
mechanics.summary: Braking early enough that the cursor finishes on target instead of through target.
cues: Brake sooner
Let the cursor arrive on target cleanly
failureModes: Overshooting and fixing it with extra cleanup movement

scenarios.name: Smooth tracking block
aliases: smooth tracking large target slow tracking
scenarios.summary: A tracking block that emphasizes continuous contact and stable speed matching.
cautions: Do not benchmark success only by pace if contact quality is unstable

evidence.claim: Tracking overshoot is often better solved by smoothness and braking quality than by more reactive aggression.
evidence.excerpt: Hand-authored seed knowledge from the initial AimMod coaching model.

entries.title: Protect quality when tracking pace fades late
entries.summary: Late-block pace fade in tracking often signals control fatigue or over-aggressive early pace that the player cannot sustain cleanly.
why: If pace collapses late without a strong accuracy gain, the player is usually spending effort inefficiently earlier in the run.
Tracking endurance is partly mechanical and partly pacing discipline.
actions: Treat the middle of the block as the scoring window and avoid overswinging the opening phase.
Shorten drill blocks temporarily if quality falls off before useful reps are finished.
Add one low-stress endurance block after the main work to build sustainable control.

drills.label: Endurance tracking
drills.reason: Lower-stress endurance reps help extend stable control without forcing chase behavior.

avoid: Judging endurance only by how long the block lasted
Do not keep extending block length if quality is already collapsing for most of the back half.

flaw.title: Late block fade
flaw.summary: The player starts with a pace they cannot sustain cleanly into the back half of the run or block.
telltales: Late-run pace falls without a real accuracy gain
Back half of the block is mostly low-quality reps
contraindications: Do not extend blocks while quality is already collapsing
avoid: Judging endurance only by how long the block lasted

mechanics.title: Block pacing discipline
mechanics.summary: The player should choose a sustainable scoring pace instead of front-loading too much intensity.
cues: Treat the middle of the block as the scoring window
Shorten blocks when quality collapses
failureModes: Early pace that cannot be sustained into the back half of the run

scenarios.name: Endurance tracking block
scenarios.summary: A lower-stress tracking block used to extend how long stable control can be maintained.
cautions: Useful only if the player still holds a real smoothness standard

evidence.claim: Late pace fade often points to pacing discipline problems rather than a simple willpower issue.
evidence.excerpt: Hand-authored seed knowledge from the initial AimMod coaching model.
